title: Bechukotai: hard words, softly
hookLine: the chapter of warnings is traditionally read quickly and quietly in synagogue

cards: Sit in a synagogue on the Shabbat this portion is read, and at one point you might notice the room change. The reader has been chanting at a steady, clear volume.
Then, partway through Leviticus twenty-six, the voice drops. The pace quickens.

The words are still audible to anyone listening closely, but they go by low and fast, like someone hurrying through a hard paragraph in a letter. At the end of that stretch, the voice comes back up to full strength.
Nobody announces it. It's a custom, and it's teaching something.

teach.b: After the blessings comes the other side. If the people refuse the covenant, the chapter lists what will follow: fear, failed harvests, enemies, exile, a land left empty.
One line says the sound of a driven leaf will send people running.
Jewish tradition calls this passage the tochacha, the rebuke, or the warning. The word shares a root with the command in Leviticus nineteen to rebuke your neighbor rather than nurse a grudge.

So how do you read a rebuke aloud to a whole congregation? The customs around it are careful. The Talmud rules that the passage of curses isn't broken into pieces; it's read as one portion, without stopping in the middle.
In many synagogues no one is called up to it by name.

teach.h: ONE READING, NO ONE SINGLED OUT.
teach.b: The reader takes it, or someone volunteers, so no one feels singled out for the curses. And it's read in that lowered, quicker voice. Not skipped.

teach.h: EVERY WORD, IN A LOW VOICE.
teach.b: Every word is read, the way you'd tell someone something hard they need to hear: without drama, without relish. The rabbis taught the same about rebuke between people. Speak, because silence can be a failure of love.
But a rebuke that shames someone in public is itself a wrong.
The tochacha is a whole chapter of hard words. The custom gives it a gentle voice.

how: In many synagogues the warnings of Leviticus 26 are read as a single unit, in a lower voice and a quicker chant; often no one is called to that reading by name, and the reader or a volunteer takes it.

games.why: the words are all read, but quietly and quickly, and often no one is called up by name for it. hard words, softly.

practice: Bring to mind one hard thing you've been avoiding, a medical result, a tough email, a critical review of your work, and don't open it yet.

Just breathe, and decide how you'll read it: slowly, all the way through, without shouting at it or at yourself. If it's something hard you need to say to someone, rehearse it in your head in a low, steady voice.

wordCard.voice: Tochacha. The rebuke: Leviticus twenty-six's warnings, read whole, in a low voice. This week ran from proclaim liberty, through guests on the land, words that wrong, and a hand that holds, to walking with God, and now this.

orig.note: Hebrew: rebuke, reproof. the name for the warning chapters of the Torah.

carryVoice: Your line: hard words, softly. Every word said, none of them shouted. That's four hundred twenty-seven days.
